name: Fatima Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. This is confidential, so please tell me both what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is a normal workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 43, and a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I write and check the inventory dashboard for warehouse customers, usually with a senior developer beside me on the hard data joins; I like seeing a stock count finally match the loading sheet. I use an AI assistant every day, but when it counts a returned box as a new one, I have to find out why before the warehouse crew loses an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the small AI helpers are useful for first drafts of stock reports. I use one daily, then compare its answer with the actual warehouse count before a customer sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools stay modest, I think my job and our mortgage are manageable. I earn a normal developer wage, my partner fixes buses on regular hours, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are a few other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the inventory dashboard and asking my senior colleague to review the tricky data joins. In the first year I'd keep using AI for draft checks on made-up records, and put 80 from each payday into the emergency account while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A wrong stock number bothers me more than a small change in the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong in the last report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it counted returned boxes as new stock. I found the mistake by checking the loading sheet, then wrote the correct test with my senior colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household expense do you plan around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are eight and eleven. We have the school bus fee in our monthly budget; I'd rather build the emergency fund slowly than promise them a bigger holiday.

think: I feel secure with **four months saved** and two regular wages.
I can see **nearby software jobs** if this firm has an ordinary setback.

Use **AI on made-up records** for draft checks, then verify results.
Save **80 each payday** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about work, while alert to stock errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI taking writing, checking, buying and customer answers could hit a junior developer before anyone admits there is a staffing change. I'd ask our staff group to count which posts are replaced and what training is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the new tools quickly, but I am still junior and sometimes need help with the hard data joins. A firm might keep one expert and a tool rather than my post; our four-month cushion protects the mortgage for a while, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group to request a written headcount and training plan from management, and attend its meeting next week. If the first year brings AI-written dashboard fixes, I'd test them on old stock records and log wrong counts; I'd also set aside an extra 40 per payday while both wages remain steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little angry at the thought of cuts being hidden behind cheerful language. I still have ways to act with my colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring into that staff meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The group includes warehouse staff who get blamed when our screen shows the wrong number. I want them at the meeting. A fast patch can send warehouse staff hunting for boxes that aren't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An extra 40 is possible while the bus depot keeps my partner's hours steady. If those hours fall, we'd keep the regular 80 if we could and drop the extra transfer first.

I know **four months saved** cannot cover the mortgage indefinitely.

fieldNote: **Junior exposure** outweighs her comfort with AI, so she fears a real income cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 reaches our stock software well before hands-on robots around 2031. I'd want paid retraining offered before a junior gets a notice, not as a promise after the wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my post could go quickly because the system would do the code and checks I am learning. My partner's bus-repair pay and four months of savings give us some room, but the mortgage and two children would still make a long search frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd list our fixed bills with my partner and ask the staff group to jointly press for a written redeployment plan. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid inventory support roles only if a vacancy exists and our combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; if no such role exists, I'd ask the local training centre about funded places before paying any fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could stay busy every evening and still watch the emergency account fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a training place already available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The training centre has courses in stock systems, but I have not been offered a place. I'd enroll only if funding covers the fee and the timetable fits school pickup and paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children the grown-ups are checking the bills and their school routine comes first. I wouldn't promise a new job until I had a signed offer.

I'd ask for **paid retraining before cuts**, not after wages stop.
think: I expect **my junior post** could go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 thinking AI gives firms years to tell us which stock checks will still need people. Robots follow around 2034 for warehouse work, but our code changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to move into checking the stock records that feed the tools, if there is a paid opening. Five years would let us add to the cushion, provided the two wages stay steady. A title alone would not pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my senior colleague to teach me one difficult data join each month and record the mistakes I find in test stock files. If the firm offers a paid inventory-audit rotation, I'd take it; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for audit jobs only if real vacancies exist and the combined pay covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because my junior wage may go before a paid audit place appears. The longer runway helps me show my work, but I would still check our savings each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a rotation real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The audit rotation would need a named supervisor and the same pay while I learn. If the firm only offers a new label and no actual duties, I'd keep doing my current dashboard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children's study plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be teenagers by then, but I wouldn't steer their studies around a guess about robots. We'd talk about what they enjoy and what we can actually afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years to 2036 lets workers prepare instead of being told on a Friday that the code has moved. Thinking AI still reaches software before 2039 robots reach hands-on work, so employers should use the time honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 53 I may have learned enough to earn in stock auditing, but I cannot guarantee those posts will exist. With our current two wages and four-month buffer, the next few years feel manageable, though I would not spend the savings on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a record of stock errors I found and continue asking for harder data joins at work. While both wages hold, we'd save 80 per payday and join our staff group each year to request a plain account of paid roles; after 2036 I'd move only for a real audit or support offer that covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and watchful about the distant change. A decade gives us room to revise the plan as the tools and our children grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your work record include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would include the returned boxes that AI counted as new stock, with customer details removed. I want future employers to see what I checked, not a claim that I can do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you avoid committing the household to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home we'd keep the present mortgage rather than borrow for a bigger place. If pay changes, we'd revisit the children's costs together before signing new debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior code work could vanish before there is a paid place for me. A written staffing plan, training funded before cuts, and real inventory-support openings would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether warehouse staff get a voice in the software plan. Warehouse staff live with our wrong counts, so I want them in the room when managers claim the new system works.

headlineQuote: Warehouse staff live with our wrong counts, so I want them in the room when managers claim the new system works.
portrait: Fatima, **43**, is a junior inventory-software developer with a two-year diploma and daily AI use.
Her **typical wage**, partner's regular bus-repair pay and four-month savings cushion support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She tests **stock reports** against loading sheets and wants warehouse staff included when the firm changes its software.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about junior cuts; fast 2028 AGI alarms her despite household savings.
With more time, she pursues **paid audit work**, supervised learning and joint staff requests, with wages covering family costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove junior code work before a paid replacement or funded course is available.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, funded training before cuts and real inventory-support vacancies would help.
